paper_a.title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis (Mildenhall et al., 2020)

metadata.description: Both learn implicit neural 3D scene representations from posed 2D images via differentiable rendering. SRN maps 3D coordinates to features and uses LSTM-based ray marching to find surfaces; NeRF maps 5D coordinates (position + direction) to density and color and uses classical volume rendering. NeRF achieves dramatically better visual quality through volumetric rendering, positional encoding, and hierarchical sampling, but both share the core paradigm of coordinate-based MLPs rendered differentiably.

matches.explanation: Both define a continuous neural scene function mapping 3D coordinates to scene properties via an MLP. NeRF: $F_\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\mathbf{c}, \sigma)$ outputs color and density. SRN: $\Phi(\mathbf{x}) \to \mathbf{f}$ outputs a feature vector. Key differences: (1) NeRF takes viewing direction as input for view-dependent appearance; SRN's scene function is view-independent (view dependence handled downstream). (2) NeRF directly outputs density/color; SRN outputs intermediate features decoded separately.

Both implement differentiable rendering to project the 3D representation to 2D images. NeRF uses classical volume rendering: integrating color weighted by density and transmittance along rays. SRN uses learned LSTM-based ray marching to find a single surface intersection point. NeRF's approach is physics-based (alpha compositing); SRN's is learned (recurrent step-size prediction). NeRF's volumetric approach handles semi-transparent and fuzzy geometry naturally; SRN's surface-based approach assumes a single surface hit.

SRN's separate pixel generator network $\Pi: \mathbf{f} \to \mathbf{c}$ that decodes features to colors is unique to SRN's architecture. In NeRF, the MLP directly outputs color $\mathbf{c}$ conditioned on viewing direction, eliminating the need for a separate decoder.

NeRF's positional encoding $\gamma(p) = (\sin(2^k \pi p), \cos(2^k \pi p))_{k=0}^{L-1}$ is a key technical innovation with no SRN counterpart. It enables the MLP to represent high-frequency details by lifting low-dimensional inputs to a high-dimensional space, overcoming the spectral bias of neural networks.

NeRF's hierarchical (coarse-to-fine) volume sampling strategy has no SRN counterpart. SRN uses a fixed number of LSTM ray marching steps, while NeRF allocates samples adaptively based on the coarse network's density estimates.

SRN's hypernetwork for per-scene conditioning (mapping latent codes to network weights) enables generalization across scenes and few-shot reconstruction. NeRF optimizes a separate MLP per scene with no cross-scene generalization mechanism. This is a major architectural difference in scope.

While both representations are implicitly 3D-structure-aware (operating in world coordinates with geometric rendering), SRN explicitly frames this as an inductive bias distinct from 2D approaches. NeRF takes this property for granted.

Both train end-to-end from posed 2D images with MSE photometric loss, using Adam optimizer. NeRF trains per-scene from scratch (~100-300k iterations). SRN can train across scenes using the hypernetwork. Both require only images and camera poses, no 3D supervision.

Both evaluate on novel view synthesis. NeRF benchmarks on Blender synthetic and LLFF real scenes; SRN benchmarks on ShapeNet categories. NeRF explicitly compares to and significantly outperforms SRN (among others) on view synthesis quality. The evaluation paradigm is the same but NeRF's results are substantially stronger.
NeRF's ablation study (isolating contributions of positional encoding, view dependence, hierarchical sampling) has no counterpart in SRN.
SRN's few-shot reconstruction and latent space interpolation experiments leverage the hypernetwork architecture and have no NeRF counterpart, since NeRF does not generalize across scenes.
